verses.text: Then Nahash the Ammonite came up, and encamped against Jabesh Gilead: and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.”
Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “On this condition I will make it with you, that all your right eyes be gouged out. I will make this dishonor all Israel.”
The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Give us seven days, that we may send messengers to all the borders of Israel; and then, if there is no one to save us, we will come out to you.”
Then the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, and spoke these words in the ears of the people, then all the people lifted up their voice, and wept.
Behold, Saul came following the oxen out of the field; and Saul said, “What ails the people that they weep?” They told him the words of the men of Jabesh.
God’s Spirit came mightily on Saul when he heard those words, and his anger burned hot.

He took a yoke of oxen, and cut them in pieces, and sent them throughout all the borders of Israel by the hand of messengers, saying, “Whoever doesn’t come out after Saul and after Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen.” The dread of Yahweh fell on the people, and they came out as one man.
He counted them in Bezek; and the children of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.
They said to the messengers who came, “Tell the men of Jabesh Gilead, ‘Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be rescued.’” The messengers came and told the men of Jabesh; and they were glad.
Therefore the men of Jabesh said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us all that seems good to you.”

On the next day, Saul put the people in three companies; and they came into the middle of the camp in the morning watch, and struck the Ammonites until the heat of the day. Those who remained were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who is he who said, ‘Shall Saul reign over us?’ Bring those men, that we may put them to death!”
Saul said, “No man shall be put to death today; for today Yahweh has rescued Israel.”
Then Samuel said to the people, “Come, and let us go to Gilgal, and renew the kingdom there.”

All the people went to Gilgal; and there they made Saul king before Yahweh in Gilgal. There they offered sacrifices of peace offerings before Yahweh; and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.

footnotes.content: Nahash brings terror to Jabesh Gilead, and the town's first instinct is to negotiate their own slavery. How quickly fear makes us believe we must purchase our survival at any cost. But deliverance was already walking toward them, in the form of a shepherd boy who hadn't yet learned his own strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To gouge out the right eye of every man — Nahash's cruelty has a purpose: to disable them as warriors, to mark them as defeated. Evil often reaches for totality, not just what it wants but what will break the spirit of those it conquers. The Lord sees this shame and He Himself will not permit it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The elders ask for seven days — a small mercy Nahash grants, perhaps in arrogance, perhaps worn by siege. But those seven days become the measure of divine timing: the thread that will connect their cry to an unexpected king and to God's intervention. Sometimes the Lord delays, not to abandon us, but to make His rescue unmistakable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The messengers arrive at Gibeah with news of exile and mutilation — and the people's response is not strategy but lament. Their weeping is honest. Grief is sometimes the truest prayer, the language the Lord honors when all else feels hollow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul comes from behind the oxen, unknowing. He had been living the simple life of a farmer's son, unaware of the crown waiting or the crisis bearing down. The Lord often finds us in the ordinary, in the middle of routine, before He calls us to become what we didn't know we needed to be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit of God comes mightily on Saul — not because he is righteous, but because this crisis needs a deliverer. His anger burns hot, and for once, that fire is kindled by God for a righteous cause. The Holy Spirit doesn't wait for perfection; He empowers the willing in their moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The yoke of oxen cut in pieces — Saul tears apart his own livelihood to send the summons. His radical act echoes a truth: deliverance requires we be willing to lose what we hold. And it works: the dread of Yahweh falls on the people, and they come out as one man. When God moves, He moves whole communities.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred thousand from Israel, thirty thousand from Judah — the numbers are staggering, a host summoned in days. Yet it is Saul's obedience to God's Spirit, not the size of the army, that matters. The Lord's victory never depends on counting heads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The messengers promise rescue by noon the next day — a deadline set by God's servant. Jabesh Gilead's despair transforms in an instant into gladness. They went from waiting to die to waiting to be saved. That shift, from surrender to hope, is what the Lord's faithfulness gives us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Jabesh now trust Saul they've never met — a trust based not on his character but on the word of his messengers and the presence of God. Real faith is often blind to the deliverer's weakness; it looks past him to the God who sent him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the morning watch, Saul strikes the Ammonites so utterly that no two are left together — Nahash's army is not merely defeated but shattered, scattered beyond recovery. The Lord's deliverance is thorough: He does not leave the enemy at our heels to threaten again tomorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the flush of victory, the people look for traitors to punish — those who had questioned Saul's kingship. Victory has a way of sharpening our desire for retribution against those who doubted. But justice in the hands of the aroused crowd can become its own kind of evil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul refuses the bloodlust and shows mercy — "No man shall be put to death today; for today Yahweh has rescued Israel." This is Saul's finest hour: he knows the victory belongs to God alone, not to him or his crown. When we truly see God's hand, we become merciful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel calls the people to Gilgal to renew the kingdom — not to establish it for the first time, but to renew it in the sight of God. The renewal happens in community, publicly, under the eye of the Lord. A kingship without that renewal would be hollow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this scene: a people gathered, a king appointed before the Lord, peace offerings made, and great rejoicing. It foreshadows the kingdom that Jesus would establish — not by earthly conquest, but by becoming the Lamb offered for all. Even Saul's flawed kingship points to a better King.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
